title: Differential of Functions
text:
This note is mainly from Multidimensional Real Analysis I by J.J.DUISTERMAAT and J.A.C.KOLK and Zorich’s Analysis I,II.
The reformulation of differential without \(\epsilon,\delta\) is due to Hadamard.

Definition 1: differentiable mapping and its differential at a point
Let \(U\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) be an open set, let \(a \in U\) and \(f:U \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^m\). Then \(f\) is said to be a differentiable mapping at \(a\) if there exists \((df)_a\in \operatorname{Lin}(\mathbb{R}^n,\mathbb{R}^m)\) such that \[
\operatorname{lim}_{x \to a}\frac{\| f(x)-f(a)-(df)_a(x-a)\Vert }{\|x-a \Vert }=0
\] \((df)_a\) is calledd the total derivative of \(f\) at \(a\) (or differential at \(a\)).



Definition 2: Version 2
A function \(f:E \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^m\) defined on a set \(E\subset \mathbb{R}^n\) is differentiable at the point \(a\in E\) which is a interior point (or weaker, limit point) of \(E\), if \[
f(a+h)-f(a)=L(a)h+\alpha(a;h)
\] where \(f(a+h)-f(a)=F(a)(-)\) may be seen as a function of variable \(h\in \{h\in \mathbb{R}^n:a+h \in E\}\equiv S_{a}\); \(L(a):\mathbb{R}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^m\) is a linear map defined on the space \(\mathbb{R}^n\); \(\alpha(a;h)\) is defined to be a function \(S_a \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^m\) such that \(\alpha(a;h)=o (h)\)



Proposition 1: Uniqueness of differential at a point
If a function \(f:E \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^m\) defined on a subset \(E \subset \mathbb{R}^n\) is differentiable at an interior point \(a\in E\) of that set, then the function has a partial derivative at that point with respect to each variable, and the differential of the function is uniquely determined by \(a\) and admits the form: \[
(df)_a(h)=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}\vert _{a} h^1+\dots+\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n}\vert _{a} h^n, \qquad h\in \mathbb{R}^n
\] Thus we know that if \(F(a)\) admits of the form of version 2, it’s uniquely written in this form.



Example 3: Differential of coordinate function
The coordinate functions \(x_i\)’s on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) are the functions which map \((a_1,\dots,a_n)\) to \(a_i\); clearly coordinate functions are differentiable at each point; thus we can define their differentials at each point, denoted by \(({dx_i})_{p}, p \in \mathbb{R}^n\); keep in mind that \(({dx_i})_p\) are just the linear mappings from \(\mathbb{R}^n\) to \(\mathbb{R}\).

title: Regular surface
text:
We will start with the most familiar example of a differentiable manifold, namely a regular surface in \(\mathbf{R}^3\). Roughly speacking, a regular surface in \(\mathbf{R}^3\) is obtained by taking pieces of a plane, deforming them, and arranging them in such a way that the resulting figure has no sharp points, edges, or self-intersections and so that it makes sense to speak of a tangent plane at points of the figure. The idea is to define a set that is, in a certain sense, two-dimensional and that also is smooth enough so that the ususal notions of calculus can be extended to it.

Definition 1
A subset \(S\subset \mathbf{R}^3\) is called a regular surface if, for each \(p\in S\), there exist a neighbourhood \(V\) of \(p\) in \(\mathbf{R}^3\) and a map \(\mathbf{x}:U\rightarrow V\cap S\) of an open set \(U\) in \(\mathbf{R}^2\) onto \(V\cap S\) such that:

\(\mathbf{x}\) is a differentiable. This means that if we write \[
\mathbf{x}=(x(u,v),y(u,v),z(u,v)), \quad (u,v)\in U
\] the functions \(x,y,z\) have continuous partial derivatives of all orders in \(U\).
\(\mathbf{x}\) is a homeomorphism. This means that \(\mathbf{x}\) has an inverse \(\mathbf{x}^{-1}:V\cap S \rightarrow U\) which is continuous.
(The regularity condition) For each \(q\in U\), the differential \((d\mathbf{x})_q:\mathbf{R}^2\rightarrow\mathbf{R}^3\) is one-to-one (injective).

The mapping \(\mathbf{x}\) is called a parametrization or a system of local coordinates in a neighbourhood of \(p\). The neighbourhood \(V\cap S\) of \(p\) in \(S\) is called a coordinate neighbourhood.


Let’s explain condition 3 by computing the Jacobian matrix of the linear map \((d\mathbf{x})_q\) in the canonical basis (the canonical basis of \(\mathbf{R}^2\) is denoted by \(\{u,v\}\)). We have : \[
\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}(q) &\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}(q) \\
\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}(q) &\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}(q) \\
\frac{\partial z}{\partial u}(q) &\frac{\partial z}{\partial v}(q) \\
\end{bmatrix}=(d\mathbf{x})_q
\] Thus the condition 3 is equivalent to saying that the rank of the matrix is \(2\) at each \(q\); i.e. one of the determinants \[
\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)},\frac{\partial(y,z)}{\partial(u,v)},\frac{\partial(x,z)}{\partial(u,v)}
\] is different from zero at each \(q\).

Remark 1
Note that the surface is created by covering \(S\) with the traces of parametrizations which satisfy conditions 1,2,3.
Condition 1 is natural as we wish to do differential geometry on the surface;
Condition 2 requires an inverse at first: this is necessary otherwise the surface may have self-intersection. Furthermore we require it to be continuous of which the necessity would be clear in the future.
Condition 3 will guarantee the existence of a tangent plane at all points of \(S\).


The most familiar example of regular surface is a sphere but we have to check condition carefully:

Exercise 1
Prove that a bilinear form \(\varphi: \mathbb{R}^3 \times \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}\) is alternate if and only if \(\varphi(v, v) = 0\), for all \(v \in \mathbb{R}^3\).



Proof. \[
\varphi(v,v)+\varphi(v,w)+\varphi(w,w)+\varphi(w,v)=\varphi(v+w,v+w)=0
\]


Exercise 2
Prove that if \(i_1 < i_2 < \ldots < i_k\) and \(j_1 < j_2 < \ldots < j_k\), then
\[
(dx_{i_1} \wedge \ldots \wedge dx_{i_k})(e_{j_1}, \ldots, e_{j_k}) =
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if } i_1 = j_1, \ldots, i_k = j_k, \\
0, & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]



Proof. \[
\begin{aligned}
& (dx_{i_1} \wedge \ldots \wedge dx_{i_k})(e_{j_1}, \ldots, e_{j_k}) \\
=&\operatorname{det}(dx_{i_s}(e_{j_t}))_{1\leq s,t \leq k}
\end{aligned}
\] If there exists some \(j_t\) is equal to none of \(i_s\), then the matrix has a zero column, \(\operatorname{det}=0\); Otherwise, \(i_1 = j_1, \ldots, i_k = j_k\) holds.


Exercise 3
Let \(\varphi\) be an exterior \(k\)-form, where \(k\) is an odd integer. Show that \(\varphi \wedge \varphi = 0\).



Proof. \[
\begin{aligned}
\varphi \wedge\varphi=(-1)^{k^2}(\varphi \wedge \varphi)
\end{aligned}
\]


Exercise 4
Let \(\varphi, \psi\) and \(\theta\) the following forms in \(\mathbb{R}^3\):
\[
\varphi = xdx - ydy,
\] \[
\psi = zdx \wedge dy + xdy \wedge dz,
\] \[
\theta = zdy.
\]
Compute: \(\varphi \wedge \psi\), \(\theta \wedge \varphi \wedge \psi\), \(d\varphi\), \(d\psi\), \(d\theta\).



Proof. \[
\begin{aligned}

&d\theta=dz \wedge dy
\end{aligned}
\]

Exercise 8: Hodge Star Operation
Given a \(k\)-form \(\omega\) in \(\mathbf{R}^{n}\) we will define an \((n - k)\)-form \(\ast \omega\) by setting
\[
\ast (d x_{i_{1}}\wedge \ldots \wedge d x_{i_{k}}) = (-1)^{\sigma}(d x_{j_{1}}\wedge \ldots \wedge d x_{j_{n - k}})
\]
and extending it linearly, where \(i_{1}< \ldots < i_{k}\), \(j_{1}< \ldots < j_{n - k}\), \((i_{1},\ldots ,i_{k},j_{1},\ldots ,j_{n - k})\) is a permutation of \((1,2,\ldots ,n)\), and \(\sigma\) is 0 or 1 according as the permutation is even or odd, respectively. Show that:

If \(\omega = a_{12}d x_{1}\wedge d x_{2} + a_{13}d x_{1}\wedge d x_{3} + a_{23}d x_{2}\wedge d x_{3}\) is a 2-form in \(\mathbf{R}^{3}\), then

\[
\star \omega = a_{12}d x_{3} - a_{13}d x_{2} + a_{23}d x_{1}.
\]

If \(\omega = a_{1}d x_{1} + a_{2}d x_{2}\) is a 1-form in \(\mathbf{R}^{2}\), then

\[
\star \omega = a_{1}d x_{2} - a_{2}d x_{1}.
\]

\(\star \star \omega = (-1)^{k(n - k)}\omega\).




Proof. 

straightforward
straightforward
Notice that \[
\begin{aligned}
&p_1:=(1,\ldots,n)\rightarrow(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j_1,\ldots,j_{n-k}) \\
&p_2:=(1,\ldots,n)\rightarrow(j_1,\ldots,j_{n-k},i_1,\ldots,i_k) \\
&p_3:=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j_1,\ldots,j_{n-k}) \rightarrow (j_1,\ldots,j_{n-k},i_1,\ldots,i_k)\\
&p_2=p_3 \circ p_1\\
&(-1)^{\sigma_1 +\sigma_2}=(-1)^{2\sigma_1+\sigma_3}=(-1)^{\sigma_3}
\end{aligned}
\] Since Moving one element from position \(k+r\) to position \(r\) (passing through \(k\) elements) requires \(k\) adjacent swaps, \((-1)^{\sigma_3}=(-1)^{(n-k)k}\).



Exercise 9: Divergence
A differentiable vector field \(\mathbf{v}\) in \(\mathbf{R}^{n}\) may be considered as a differentiable map \(v:\mathbf{R}^{n}\to \mathbf{R}^{n}\). We will define a function \(\operatorname{div} v:\mathbf{R}^{n}\to \mathbf{R}\) (to be called the divergence of \(v\)) as follows:
\[
(\operatorname{div}v)(p) = \operatorname{trace}(dv)_{p},\quad p\in \mathbf{R}^{n},
\]
where \((dv)_{p}:\mathbf{R}_{p}^{n}\to \mathbf{R}_{p}^{n}\) is the differential of \(\mathbf{v}\) at \(p\). Show that:

If \(v = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{i} e_{i}\), where \(\{e_{i}\}\) is the canonical basis of \(\mathbf{R}^{n}\), then

\[
\operatorname{div}v = \sum \frac{\partial a_{i}}{\partial x_{i}}.
\]

If \(\omega\) denotes the differential 1-form obtained from \(\mathbf{v}\) by the canonical isomorphism induced by the inner product \(\langle , \rangle\) and \(\nu\) is the volume element of \(\mathbf{R}^{n}\) (Exercise 9), the divergence can be obtained as follows: \[
v \longrightarrow \omega \longrightarrow \star \omega \longrightarrow d(\star \omega) = (\operatorname{div}v)\nu,
\]




Proof. 

\[
(\operatorname{div}v)(p)=\operatorname{trace}(dv)_{p}=\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial a_{i}}{\partial x_{i}} \vert_{p}
\] since \(v=\sum_{i=1}^n a_ie_i\) where \(a_i:\mathbf{R}^n \rightarrow \mathbf{R}\) is differentiable.
Notice that \(\omega=\langle v,- \rangle=\sum a_i\langle e_i, - \rangle=\sum a_i dx_i\); it follows that \[
\begin{aligned}
&^{\star}(\sum a_i dx_i)=\sum a_i (^{\star}dx_i)\\
&d(a_i) \wedge (^{\star}dx_i)=\sum \frac{\partial a_i}{\partial x_i}dx_1\wedge \ldots \wedge dx_n \\
&(\sum \frac{\partial a_i}{\partial x_i})dx_1\wedge \ldots \wedge dx_n = \operatorname{trace}(dv)\nu=(\operatorname{div}v)\nu
\end{aligned}
\]



Exercise 10: Gradiant
Given a differentiable function \(f:\mathbf{R}^{n}\to \mathbf{R}\), define a vector field \(\operatorname{grad} f\) in \(\mathbf{R}^{n}\) (the gradient of \(f\)) by
\[
\langle \operatorname{grad} f(p),u\rangle = (df)_{p}(u),\quad \text{for all } p\in \mathbf{R}^{n} \text{ and all } u\in \mathbf{R}_{p}^{n}.
\]
Notice that \(\operatorname{grad} f\) is the vector field corresponding to the 1-form \(df\) in the canonical isomorphism. Show that:

In the canonical basis \(\{e_{i}\}\) of \(\mathbf{R}^{n}\),

\[
\operatorname{grad} f = \sum \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}} e_{i}.
\]

If \(p\in \mathbf{R}^{n}\) is such that \(\operatorname{grad} f(p)\neq 0\), then \(\operatorname{grad} f(p)\) is perpendicular to the “level surface” \(\{q\in \mathbf{R}^{n}; f(q) = f(p)\}\).
The linear map \((df)_{p}:\mathbf{R}_{p}^{n}\to \mathbf{R}\) restricted to the unit sphere with center at \(p\) reaches its maximum for \(v = \operatorname{grad} f / |\operatorname{grad} f|\).




Proof. A vector field \(\mathbf{v}\) is uniquely determined by the linear forms \(\langle \mathbf{v}(p),- \rangle \in (\mathbf{R}_p^{n})^*\).

\[
\begin{aligned}
&(\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}} e_{i})(p)=\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}}\vert_p e_{i} \\
\Rightarrow &[(\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}} e_{i})(p)](u)=\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}}\vert_p u_{i} \\
&=(df)_p(u)
\end{aligned}
\] Hence, \(\operatorname{grad} f = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}} e_{i}\).
Let \(\gamma: (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \to S\) be any smooth curve with \(\gamma(0) = p\). Since \(\gamma(t) \in S\) for all \(t\),

\[
f(\gamma(t)) = f(p), \quad \forall t \in (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon).
\]
Differentiating with respect to \(t\) and applying the chain rule gives
\[
(df)_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t)) = 0.
\]
At \(t=0\),
\[
(df)_p(\gamma'(0)) = 0.
\]
By the definition of the gradient, \(\langle \operatorname{grad} f(p), u \rangle = (df)_p(u)\) for all \(u \in \mathbf{R}_p^n\). Taking \(u = \gamma'(0)\),
\[
\langle \operatorname{grad} f(p), \gamma'(0) \rangle = 0.
\]
Thus \(\operatorname{grad} f(p) \perp \gamma'(0)\). Since \(\gamma'(0)\) is an arbitrary tangent vector to \(S\) at \(p\), the gradient is orthogonal to every tangent direction, hence perpendicular to the level surface \(S\).

By 1, we have \[
\Vert (df)_p(u) \Vert= \Vert \operatorname{grad}f(p) \cdot u   \Vert \leq \Vert \operatorname{grad}f(p) \Vert \cdot \Vert u   \Vert
\] and the equality holds when \(u\parallel \operatorname{grad}f(p)\); thus \(u=\operatorname{grad}f(p)/\vert \operatorname{grad}f(p)\vert\) where \((df)_p\) attains its maximum on the unit sphere.



Exercise 11: Laplacian
Given a differentiable function \(f:\mathbf{R}^{n}\to \mathbf{R}\), we will define the Laplacian \(\Delta f:\mathbf{R}^{n}\to \mathbf{R}\) by
\[
\Delta f = \operatorname{div}(\operatorname{grad} f).
\]
Show that:

\[
\Delta f = \sum \frac{\partial^{2} f}{\partial x_{i}^{2}},
\]
\[
\Delta (fg) = f\Delta g + g\Delta f + 2\langle \operatorname{grad} f, \operatorname{grad} g \rangle,
\]
\(d * (df) = (\Delta f)\nu\), where \(\nu\) is the volume element of \(\mathbf{R}^{n}\).




Proof. 

\[
\Delta f = \operatorname{div}(\operatorname{grad} f)=\operatorname{div}(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\cfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}e_i)=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{\partial^2f}{\partial x_i^2}
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta (fg)&=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial^2(fg)}{\partial x_i^2}=\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}(f\frac{\partial g}{\partial x_i}+g\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}) \\
&=\sum_{i=1}^nf\frac{\partial^2 g}{\partial x_i^2}+g\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i^2}+2\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}\frac{\partial g}{\partial x_i} \\
&=f \Delta g +g \Delta f+2 \langle \operatorname{grad}f,\operatorname{grad} g \rangle
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
d (^{\star} df)=d(^{\star}(\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}dx_i))=(\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i^2})\nu
\]



Exercise 12: Rotational
Let \(v\) be a differentiable vector field in \(\mathbf{R}^{n}\). The rotational \(\operatorname{rot} v\) is the \((n - 2)\)-form defined by:
\[
v \longmapsto \omega \longrightarrow d\omega \longrightarrow *(d\omega) = \operatorname{rot} v,
\]

Prove that \(\operatorname{rot}(\operatorname{grad} f) = 0\).
In the particular case when \(n = 3\), the \((n-2)=1\)-form \(\operatorname{rot} v\) corresponds to a vector field which is also denoted by \(\operatorname{rot} v\). Show that, for \(n = 3\):

\operatorname{rot}(\sum_{i=1}^3a_ie_i)=(\frac{\partial a_3}{\partial x_2}-\frac{\partial a_2}{\partial x_3})e_1+(\frac{\partial a_1}{\partial x_3}-\frac{\partial a_3}{\partial x_1})e_2+(\frac{\partial a_2}{\partial x_1}-\frac{\partial a_1}{\partial x_2})e_3
\]
\(\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{rot} v) = 0\).




Proof. 

\(\operatorname{rot}(\operatorname{grad} f)=^{\star}(d^2f)=0\)

Straightforward.
\[
\operatorname{div}((\frac{\partial a_3}{\partial x_2}-\frac{\partial a_2}{\partial x_3})e_1)=
\frac{\partial^2 a_3}{\partial x_1 \partial x_2}-\frac{\partial^2 a_2}{\partial x_1 \partial x_3}

Exercise 13: A geometric definition of the \(\star\) operation
An element \(\phi \in \Lambda^{k}(\mathbf{R}_{p}^{n})^{*}\) is called decomposable if \(\phi = \phi_{1}\wedge \ldots \wedge \phi_{k}\), where \(\phi_{i}\), \(i = 1,\ldots ,k\), are linearly independent elements of \(\Lambda^{1}(\mathbf{R}_{p}^{n})^{*}\simeq (\mathbf{R}_{p}^{n})^{*}\). Prove that:

If \(\phi_{i} = \sum_{j} a_{i j}\beta_{j}\), \(i = 1,\ldots ,k\), \(\beta_{j}\in (\mathbf{R}_{p}^{n})^{*}\), and \(\det(a_{i j}) = 1\), then \(\phi_{1}\wedge \ldots \wedge \phi_{k} = \beta_{1}\wedge \ldots \wedge \beta_{k}\); thus, a decomposable element may have more than one representation.
If \(\phi_{1}\wedge \ldots \wedge \phi_{k} = \beta_{1}\wedge \ldots \wedge \beta_{k} = \phi\) are two representations of \(\phi\), then \(\phi_{i} = \sum_{j} a_{i j}\beta_{j}\), with \(\det(a_{i j}) = 1\).







Tip 1





Hint: Extend the \(\beta_{j}\) into a basis \(\beta_{1},\ldots ,\beta_{k},\beta_{k + 1},\ldots \beta_{n}\) of \((\mathbf{R}_{p}^{n})^{*}\) and write   \[
\phi_{i} = \sum_{j} a_{i j}\beta_{j} + \sum_{\eta} b_{i\eta}\beta_{\eta},\qquad \eta = k + 1,\ldots ,n.
\] 
Notice that \(\beta_{1}\wedge \dots \wedge \beta_{k}\wedge \phi_{i} = \phi_{1}\wedge \dots \wedge\phi_{k}\wedge \phi_{i} = 0\). This implies that   \[
\sum_{\eta} b_{i\eta}\beta_{1}\wedge \ldots \wedge \beta_{k}\wedge \beta_{\eta} = 0,
\] 
and since \(\beta_{1}\wedge \ldots \wedge \beta_{k}\wedge \beta_{\eta}\) are linearly independent, \(b_{i\eta} = 0\). 




If \(\phi = \phi_{1}\wedge \ldots \wedge \phi_{k}\) is decomposable, the vectors \(v_{1},\ldots ,v_{k}\in \mathbf{R}_{p}^{n}\), where \(v_{i}\leftrightarrow \phi_{i}\) is the correspondence induced by the inner product \(\langle , \rangle\) of \(\mathbf{R}^{n}\), are linearly independent, and the subspace of \(\mathbf{R}^{n}\) generated by them does not depend on the representation of \(\phi\). This will be called the subspace of \(\phi\).
If \(\phi = \phi_{1}\wedge \ldots \wedge \phi_{k}\) is decomposable, the \(k\)-volume of the solid generated by \(v_{1},\ldots ,v_{k}\) does not depend on the representation of \(\phi\). This will be called the volume of \(\phi\).

5.If \(\phi = \phi_{1}\wedge \ldots \wedge \phi_{k}\) is decomposable, define \(\ast \phi\) as an element of \(\Lambda^{n - k}(\mathbf{R}_{p}^{n})^{*}\) with the following properties:

the subspace of \(\ast \phi\) is perpendicular to the subspace of \(\phi\).
the volume of \(\ast \phi\) is equal to the volume of \(\phi\).
\(\phi \wedge \ast \phi\) is positive, i.e., its value in a positive basis of \(\mathbf{R}_{p}^{n}\) is positive.
Prove that \(\ast \phi\) is well defined.







Tip 2





 Hint: Let \(v_{i}\leftrightarrow \phi_{i}\), \(i = 1,\ldots ,k\), as in (c) and let \(W\) be the subspace of \(\mathbf{R}_{p}^{n}\) generated by the \(v_{i}\)’s. In \(W^{\perp}\) consider an orthonormal basis \(e_{k + 1},\ldots ,e_{n}\) so that the basis \(v_{1},\ldots ,v_{k},e_{k + 1},\ldots ,e_{n}\) of \(\mathbf{R}_{p}^{n}\) is positive. Define \(\phi_{j}\in (\mathbf{R}_{p}^{n})^{*}, j = k + 1,\ldots ,n\), by the correspondence \(\phi_{j}\leftrightarrow e_{j}\) mentioned in (c), and let \(\lambda >0\) be the volume of \(W\). Check that \(\lambda \, \phi_{k + 1}\wedge \ldots \wedge \phi_{n}\) satisfies 1, 2 and 3.




Let \(v_{1},v_{2}\) be two vectors in \(\mathbf{R}^{3}\) and let \(\phi_{1}\leftrightarrow v_{1},\phi_{2}\leftrightarrow v_{2}\) be the one-forms given by the correspondence in (c). Define the vector product \(v_{1}\times v_{2}\leftrightarrow \ast (\phi_{1}\wedge \phi_{2})\) and describe geometrically the vector \(v_{1}\times v_{2}\).
A \(k\)-form \(\omega\) in \(\mathbf{R}^{n}\) is decomposable if \(\omega(p)\) is decomposable for each \(p\in \mathbf{R}^{n}\). Every \(k\)-form in \(\mathbf{R}^{n}\) is a linear combination of decomposable \(k\)-forms of the type \(d x_{i_{1}}\wedge \ldots \wedge d x_{i_{k}}\). Show that with the above definition, \(\ast (d x_{i_{1}}\wedge \ldots \wedge d x_{i_{k}})\) gives the same expression as in Exercise 10.




Proof. 

\[
\varphi_1 \wedge \ldots \wedge \varphi_k=(\sum a_{1j}\beta_j)\wedge\ldots\wedge(\sum a_{nj}\beta_j)=\operatorname{det}(a_{ij})\beta_1\wedge\ldots\wedge\beta_k
\]

\]

&=\int_0^1 a(tx,ty,tz)\,dt+\int_0^1 t\,(xa_1+yb_1+zc_1)\,dt \\

\end{aligned}
\]
\[

title: Affine and finite morphisms
text:
A morphism between varieties \(f:X \rightarrow Y\) is affine if there is an open cover \(Y=\cup U_i\) by affines \(U_i\) such that the open subsets \(f^{-1}(U_i)\) of \(X\) are affine.
If we furthermore choose the cover such that each \(\mathcal{O}_{X}(f^{-1}(U_i))\) is a \(\mathcal{O}_{Y}(U_i)\)-module of finite type then the morphism \(f\) is said to be finite;more precisely, \[
f_i^*: \mathcal{O}_{Y}(U_i) \rightarrow \mathcal{O}_{X}(f^{-1}(U_i))
\] is a homomorphism of finite type.
If \(Y\) is a point \(P\), \(f:X \rightarrow Y\) is affine if and only if \(X\) is affine and \(f:X \rightarrow P\) is finite if and only if \(X\) is a finite set.
As for embedding we have

Lemma 1

Let \(i:X\hookrightarrow Y\) be the inclusion of a closed subvariety. Then \(i\) is finite.
Let \(f\) be a regular function on a variety \(X\). Then the inclusion \(j:D(f)\rightarrow X\) is affine.



At first, let’s review the structure of a closed subsapce in an affine variety. (the proof is here)

Reminder 1
Let \(X\) be an affine variety.

Denote the \(k\)-algebra of all the (global) regular functions on \(X\) by \(A\) and let \(Y \subset X\) be a closed subset; Denote the ideal of functions vanishing on \(Y\) by \(I\); Then the charaterization of \(Y\) is \[
\begin{aligned}
Y \cong \operatorname{Spec}(A/I); \quad \mathcal{O}_{X}(Y) \cong A/I
\end{aligned}
\]
A subsapce \(Y\subseteq X\) is an affine variety if and only if it’s closed.




Proof. 

\(i\) is affine for \(i^{-1}(U)=U\cap X\) where \(U\subset Y\) is any open affine is a closed subspace of the affine variety \(U\). Denote the ideal of \(\mathcal{O}_{X}(U)\) vanishing on \(U\cap X\) by \(\mathcal{I}(U\cap X)\); then by Reminder, we have
\[
\mathcal{O}_{X}(U\cap X) \cong \mathcal{O}_{X}(U)/\mathcal{I}(U\cap X)
\] thus \(\mathcal{O}_{X}(U\cap X)\) is a \(\mathcal{O}_X(U)\)-module of finite type where the generator is just \(1 \,(\operatorname{mod}\, \mathcal{I}(U\cap X))\).
Restrict \(f\) to \(U\); we obtain that \(D(f)\cap U=D(f\restriction_{U})\) and thus we have \(D(f\restriction_{U})\cong \operatorname{Spec} ([\mathcal{O}_X(U)]_{f\restriction_U})\) which is affine.

text:
Topological properties of finite morphisms
Topologically finite morphisms are special.

Lemma 2
Let \(f:X \rightarrow Y\) be a finite morphism. Let \(Z\) be a closed subset of \(X\). Then its image \(f(Z)\) is closed.



Proof. As the property is local on \(Y\) we may assume that \(X\) and \(Y\) are affine and thus \(\mathcal{O}(X)\) is a \(\mathcal{O}(Y)\)-module of finite type. As \(Z\) is closed, we have the surjection \(i^*:\mathcal{O}(X)\rightarrow \mathcal{O}(Z)\). Let \(I\) be the kernel of the composition \(\psi\): \[
\mathcal{O}(Y) \xrightarrow{f^*}\mathcal{O}(X)\xrightarrow{i^*}\mathcal{O}(Z)
\] Then we have an inclusion: \[
A=\mathcal{O}(Y)/I \hookrightarrow \mathcal{O}(Z)=B
\] and \(B\) is an \(A\)-module of finite type.
By definition a point \(y\) of \(Y\) is contained in the image \(f(Z)\) if and only if \(\delta_{y}:\mathcal{O}(Y)\rightarrow k\) is the composition of \(\psi\) with \(\delta_z:\mathcal{O}(Z)\rightarrow k\) for some \(z\) in \(Z\).

Details 1
\[
\begin{aligned}
&y=f(z) \iff \delta_y=\delta_{f(z)} \quad \text{notice that here } Y \cong \operatorname{Spec}(A) \text{ for some algebra } A \text{ as } Y \text{ is affine } \\
& \delta_{f(z)}= \delta_z \circ \psi \quad \text{ for: } \\
&\delta_{f(z)}(h)=(h\circ f)(z)=(h\circ f\circ i)(z) \\
&(\delta_z \circ \psi)(h)=(i^* \circ f^*)(h)(z)=(h\circ f \circ i)(z) \\
& \Rightarrow \delta_y=\delta_z \circ \psi
\end{aligned}
\]


thus \(f(Z)\subset \operatorname{zeores}(I)\) and it suffices to show the reverse inclusion now. In other words if \(y\) is in \(\operatorname{zeroes}(I)\) then \(\delta_y\) factor into the homomorphism \(\overline{\delta_y}:A \rightarrow k\) by the first isomorphism theroem. By Lemma there is a homomorphism \(\delta_z:B \rightarrow k\) where \(z\) is a point of \(Z\) which can be extended to \(\overline{\delta_y}\); thus \(f(y)=z\), and we are done.

Let’s explain and visualize this proof using commutative diagram:


    
    

We have another property of finite morphisms

Lemma 3
Let \(f:X \rightarrow Y\) be a finite morphism and let \(Z_1\subsetneq Z_2\) be two closed subsets of \(X\) where \(Z_2\) is irreducible. Then \(f(Z_1)\subsetneq f(Z_2)\).


Before we prove this let us see what it says in a special case.

Corollary 4
If \(f:X \rightarrow Y\) is a finite morphism and \(y\) is a point of \(Y\) then the fiber \(f^{-1}(y)\) is finite.








Tipproof of Corollary





As \(f^{-1}(y)\subseteq X\) is a subspace of a noetherian space \(X\), it’s also a noetherian space. Thus it will suffice to show that each irreducible component \(Z_i\) of \(f^{-1}(y)\) is finite. Let \(z\) be a point of \(Z_i\). Let \(Z_i^\prime=\{z\}\). Then \(f(Z_i)=f(Z_i^\prime)=\{y\}\). Hence \(Z_i=Z_i^\prime\).




Proof. It suffices to show that the affine case; then \(\mathcal{O}(X)\) is a \(\mathcal{O}(Y)\)-module of finite type. Furthermore, we may assume that \(Z_2=X\) is irreducible and \(Y=f(X)\). Thus \(\mathcal{O}(X)\) is an integral domain and is finitely generated as a module over the ring \(\mathcal{O}(Y)\).
We need to show that there is a non-constant regular function \(g\) on \(Y\) such that \(f^*(g)\) vanishes on \(Z_1\) because this will show that \(f(Z_1) \subset \operatorname{zeroes}(g) \subsetneq f(X)=Y\).
As \(Z_1\subsetneq X\) is closed, there is a non-constant regular function \(h\) on \(X\) which vanishes on \(Z_1\). Consider the \(\mathcal{O}(Y)\)-submodule of \(\mathcal{O}(X)\) generated by \(\{h^i:i\in \mathbb{N}\}\). This is finitely generated over \(\mathcal{O}(Y)\) because \(\mathcal{O}(Y)\) is noetherian (\(\operatorname{f.g.}\,k\text{-}\) algebra) and \(\mathcal{O}(X)\) is a \(\mathcal{O}(Y)\)-module of finite type. Then for \(i>>0\), \(h^i=\sum_{0\leq j<i}(f^*g_j)h^j\) where \(g_j\in \mathcal{O}(Y)\). We may assume that \(g_0\neq 0\). Thus \(f^*g_0\) vanishes on \(Z_1\). \(g_0\) is the non-constant regular function as expected.

title: The Hilbert basis theorem
text:
A ring \(A\) is noetherian if any ideal of \(A\) is finitely generated.

Proposition 1
A ring \(A\) is noetherian if and only if the following property holds:
Any submodule of a finitely generated \(A\)-module \(M\) is finitely generated.



Proof. Only need to show that the direction \(\Rightarrow\); we use the induction on the number \(n\) of generators of \(M\).

\(n=1\); then submodule of \(M=A\,x\) admits the form \(I\,x\) where \(I\) is an ideal of \(A\); as \(I\) is f.g., so is \(I\,x\).
suppose the proposition holds for \(n=k\)
\(n=k+1\); suppose that \(M=\sum_{i=1}^{k+1} A\, e_i\), \(N=\sum_{i=1}^{k} A\, e_i\) and \(K \subset M\) is a submodule;


\(N\cap K\) is clearly a submodule of \(N\); by the induction hypothesis, \(N \cap K\) is f.g. \(A\)-module, say \(A\,t_1+\dots+A\,t_s\)
hence we wish to find out the generators left;let us divide out the submodule \(N\cap K\) in \(K\) and observe that:
\[
\frac{K}{N\cap K} \cong \frac{N+K}{N} \subseteq \frac{M}{N} \cong A\,e_{k+1}\,(\operatorname{mod} N)
\]
by 1 and the isomorphism, we know the submodule \(\frac{K}{N\cap K}\) is finitely generated, say \(A\,v_1+\dots+A\,v_t\).
let us use the lifting technique; choose representations \(k_i \in K\) such that \(v_i=k_i\, \operatorname{mod}{N\cap K}\)
It’s straightforward to check that \(t_1,\dots,t_s,k_1,\dots,k_t\) generate \(K\); thus \(K\) is a finitely generated \(A\)-module.


Notice the follwing counterexample (non-Noetherian ring):






Warning



Let \(R=\mathbb{Z}[X_1,\dots,X_n,\dots]\) and \(M=R\); then clearly \(M\) is a finitely generated \(R\)-module. However, the submodule \(N=(X_1,\dots,X_n,\dots)\) is not finitely generated as a \(R\)-module.



Proof. The elements in \(N\) are polynomials without constant terms in finitely many variables. Assume that there exists a system of finite generators \(f_1,\dots,f_k\) and the biggest index of variables in these generators is \(m\); then \(X_{m+1}\) admits a form: \[
X_{m+1}=\sum_{i=1}^{k} g_if_i, \qquad g_i\in \mathbb{Z}[X_1,\dots,X_n,\dots],\,f_i\in\mathbb{Z}[X_1,\dots,X_m]
\] Let \[
X_i
\begin{cases}
&\to0;i \neq m+1 \\
&\to1;i=m+1
\end{cases}
\] thus we get the contradiction: \[
1=\sum g_i(0,\dots,1,\dots)f_i(0,\dots,0)=0
\]

Let \(R=\mathbb{Z}[X_1,\dots,X_n,\dots]\) and \(M=R\); then clearly \(M\) is a finitely generated \(R\)-module. However, the submodule \(N=(X_1,\dots,X_n,\dots)\) is not finitely generated as a \(R\)-module.



Proof. The elements in \(N\) are polynomials without constant terms in finitely many variables. Assume that there exists a system of finite generators \(f_1,\dots,f_k\) and the biggest index of variables in these generators is \(m\); then \(X_{m+1}\) admits a form: \[
X_{m+1}=\sum_{i=1}^{k} g_if_i, \qquad g_i\in \mathbb{Z}[X_1,\dots,X_n,\dots],\,f_i\in\mathbb{Z}[X_1,\dots,X_m]
\] Let \[
X_i
\begin{cases}
&\to0;i \neq m+1 \\
&\to1;i=m+1
\end{cases}
\] thus we get the contradiction: \[
1=\sum g_i(0,\dots,1,\dots)f_i(0,\dots,0)=0
\]

title: The Hilbert basis theorem
text:
Hilbert Basis Theorem

Theorem 2
A finitely generated \(k\)-algebra \(A\) is noetherian.



Proof. Let \(\psi:k[X_1,\dots,X_n]\rightarrow A\) be a surjection. Let \(I\) be an ideal of \(A\). To show that \(I\) is finitely generated it sufffices to show the same for the ideal \(I^\prime=\psi^{-1}(I)\unlhd k[X_1,\dots,X_n]\). If \(I^\prime=0\) there is no problem; otherwise there exists a non-zero polynomial \(f\) in \(I^\prime\). By Noether’s normalisation lemma, we may assume that \(f\) is monic in \(X_n\).
By induction we may assume that \(k[X_1,\dots,X_{n-1}]=B\) is noetherian. Consider \(I^\prime/(f) \subseteq k[X_1,\dots,X_n]/(f)\). This is a \(B\)-submodule of a \(B\)-module which is finitely generated. Then lift these generators to \(I\prime\) and we know that \(I^\prime\) is a finitely generated \(B\)-module; thus noetherian.

Next we show the lemma used before; by the previous reasoning we only need to show the following lemma:

Lemma 3
An open subset \(U\) of an affine variety \(\operatorname{Spec} \, A\) is quasi-compact.



Proof. Let \(U=\bigcup D(f_i)\) for \(f_i\) in \(A\). Then the complement of \(U\) is \[
\operatorname{zeores}((f_i))=\operatorname{zeroes}((f_{i_1}),\dots,f_{i_r})
\] for some finite number \(r\) by Hilbert basis theorem and definition of noetherian ring;
Thus \(U=D(f_{i_1})\cup\ldots\cup D(f_{i_r})\) is a finite subcovering.

title: The Hilbert basis theorem
text:
Noetherian Topology
A topological space such that every open subset is quasi-compact is called noetherian. As a variety is the finite union of open affines, we have proved that :

Theorem 4
Any variety has a noetherian topology.


There is a chain condition that charaterizes noetherian space.

Lemma 5
Let \(X\) be a topological space. Then \(X\) is noetherian if and only if any descending chain \(X_1\supseteq X_2 \supseteq \dots\) of closed subsets becomes stationary eventually: \(X_r=X_{r+1}=\dots\) for some \(r\).



Proof. Assume that \(X\) is noetherian and we have an arbitrary descending chain \(X_i\) of closed subsets. The open set \(U=X-\cap X_i\) is quasi-compact. Now \(U\) has the chain \(X_1\cap U \supseteq X_2\cap U \supseteq \dots\) of closed subsets which has empty intersection. Thus \(X_r\cap U=\emptyset\) for some \(r\) as \(U\) is quasi-compact; this means \(X_r \subseteq \cap X_i\) and thus \(X_r=X_{r+1}=\dots\).
Conversely suppose that \(U\) is not quasi-compact, then there exists \(U_1\supseteq U_2 \supseteq\dots\) which is a infinite descending chain of closed subsets of \(U\) such that \(\cap U_i=\emptyset\); Consider \(X_i=\text{ closure of } U_i \subseteq X\); If any descending chain of closed subsets is stationary, then \(X_r=X_{r+1}=\dots\) for some \(r\). As \(U_i=U \cap X_i\), we have \(\cap U_i=U_r=\emptyset\); Contradiction.

title: Determinantial Varieties
text:
Let \(X\) be a variety. Consider a matrix \(\alpha=(\alpha_j^i)\) where the coefficients \(\alpha_j^i\) are regular functions on \(X\). For each point \(x\) of \(X\) we can think of \(\alpha(x)\equiv (\alpha_j^i(x))\) as the matrix of a linear transformation \(\hat{\alpha}(x):V \to W\) between two \(k\)-vector spaces. By assumption the matrix \(\alpha(x)\) depends regular on \(x\).
Let \(r\) be an integer. Consider the subset \(D_r(\alpha)=\{x\in X: \operatorname{rank}(\alpha(x)) \leq r\}\) of \(X\).






NoteLemma



\(D_r(\alpha)\) is a closed subvariety of \(X\).



Proof. Let \(I_r(\alpha)\) be the set of all determinants of all \((r+1) \times (r+1)\) submatrices of \(\alpha\). Then \(I_r(\alpha)\) consists of regular functions on \(X\) and \(x \in D_r(\alpha) \iff f(x)=0\) for all \(f \in I_r(\alpha)\). Thus \(D_r(\alpha)\) is closed.


Example

If \(\alpha=(f_1,\dots,f_s)\) is just a \((1\times s)\) matrix, \(D_0({\alpha})=\{x:f_i(x)=0,1\leq i \leq s\}\)
If \(r=\operatorname{min}(m,n)-1\) (wlog let \(n \leq m\)), \(D_{r}(\alpha)=\{x:\operatorname{det}(M_{n\times n}(x))=0\}\)







NoteDefinition



Let \(f:X \to \mathbb{R}\cup \{+\infty\}\), \(f\) is said to be lower-semicontinuous if for any real number \(\alpha\), \(\{x:f(x) > \alpha\}\) is always open or equivalently \(\{x:f(x) \leq \alpha\}\) is always closed.


One way to restate the lemma is






TipCorollary



The function \(\operatorname{rank}(\alpha(x))\) on \(X\) is lower-semicontinuous.

title: The rest of the proof of existence of affine varieties/subvarieties
text:
Again, we assume the base field \(k\) is an algebraically closed in this section.
We will first show the following result:
\[
\text{The subring } A \subseteq \mathcal{O}(\Spec A) \ \text{is all of } \mathcal{O}(\Spec A).
\]
in other words, we have \[
A \cong \mathcal{O}(\Spec A)
\] where \(A\) is a finitely-generate \(k\)-algebra which has no nilpotents.






ImportantProof



Let \(f(x)\) be a function in \(\mathcal{O}(\Spec A)\). We need to verify that \(f\) is in \(A\). By definition, we have an open cover \(\Spec A=\bigcup U_{\alpha}\) by open subsets such that \(f(u)=\tfrac{g_{\alpha}(u)}{h_{\alpha}(u)}\) when \(u\) in \(U_{\alpha}\) where \(g_{\alpha},h_{\alpha}\) are in \(A\) and \(h_{\alpha}(u)\) is never zero on \(U_{\alpha}\). We may assume that \(U_{\alpha}=D(k_{\alpha})\) for some \(k_{\alpha} \in A\). Doing the rename \[
f(u)=\frac{(k_{\alpha}g_{\alpha})(u)}{(k_{\alpha}h_{\alpha})(u)}  \text{ on } D(k_{\alpha}\cdot h_{\alpha})=D(K_{\alpha})
\] We may assume that \(h_{\alpha}=k_{\alpha}\).
Next consider the function \(h_{\alpha}^{2}f\). This equals \(h_{\alpha}g_{\alpha}\) on \(D(h_{\alpha})\) as \[
h_{\alpha}^{2}f=h_{\alpha}^{2} \cdot \frac{g_{\alpha}}{h_{\alpha}}=h_{\alpha}g_{\alpha} \text{ on } U_{\alpha}
\]
Moreover both of them vanish outside \(U_{\alpha}\), and thus \(h_{\alpha}^{2}f \equiv h_{\alpha}g_{\alpha}\) as functions on the whole \(\Spec A\) and
Since \(\Spec A=\bigcup{D(h_\alpha)}\), by the corollary in the last section, it follows that \[
1_{A}=\sum_{\text{finite}}a_{\alpha}h_{\alpha}^{2}
\] for some \(a_{\alpha} \in A\). Therefore we have (use the technique called partition of unity where the result above comes into play): \[
f=f \cdot 1_{A}=\sum_{\text{finite}}a_{\alpha}(fh_{\alpha}^{2}) \equiv \sum_{\text{finite}}a_{\alpha}h_{\alpha}g_{\alpha}
\] which is a function in \(A\). We have thus proved that any global regular function in \(\mathcal{O}(\Spec A)\) is in \(A\).


It remains to show that \(\Spec A\) is affine, i.e.






ImportantTheorem



\[
\operatorname{Mor}(X,\Spec A) \xrightarrow{*} \operatorname{Hom}_{k}(A,\mathcal{O}(X))
\] is a bijection.








NoteProof



Let \(\delta_{x}:\mathcal{O}(X) \to k\) be evaluation of a function at a point \(x\). Let \(f:X \to \Spec A\) be a morphism. Let \(a\) be an element of A (treated as the \(k\)-algebra consisting of functions) and \(x\) be a point of \(X\). Then, by definiton of \(f^{*}\), \(a(f(x))=(f^*a)(x)\), or, rather, \(\delta_{f(x)}\) is the composition \[
A\xrightarrow{f^{*}}\mathcal{O}(X)\xrightarrow{\delta_{x}}k
\] It follows that \(f \neq g \rightarrow f^{*} \neq g^{*}\) as \[
f^{*}=g^{*} \Rightarrow  \delta_{x}\circ g^{*}= \delta_{x} \circ f^{*} \iff \delta_{f(x)}=\delta_{g(x)} \iff f=g
\] The last equality holds because that \[
\delta_{f(x)}(a)=\delta_{A\xrightarrow{f(x)}k}(a)=f(x)(a)
\] i.e the point \(f(x)\) is the same as the homomorphism \(\delta_{f(x)}\). Thus we have proved that \(*\) is injective.
Conversely let \(\phi:A \rightarrow \mathcal{O}(X)\) be a \(k\)-algebra homomorphism. Define \(f \equiv r(\phi)\) by the formula \(\delta_{f(x)}=\delta_{x}\circ \phi\). We shall show that \(f\) is a morphism.






NoteExercise



Proof:
As \(f^{-1}(D(h))=\{x\in X : \phi (h)(x) \neq0\}\) where \(h \in A\), \(f\) is continuous.
Assume that \(h\) admits a form \(a(x)/b(x), a,b \in A\) on \(\mathcal{O}_{\Spec A}(D(b))\) and we expect that \(h\circ f \in \mathcal{O}_{X}(f^{-1}(D(b)))\).
Indeed we have \[(h \circ f)(x)=h(f(x))=h(\delta_{x} \circ \phi)=\frac{a(\delta_{x} \circ \phi)}{b(\delta_{x} \circ \phi)}=\frac{\phi(a)(x)}{\phi(b)(x)} \in \mathcal{O}_{X}(f^{-1}(D(b)))
\]


Clearly \(r \circ * = \operatorname{id}_{\operatorname{Mor}(X,\Spec A)}\) as \[
(r \circ *) (f)(x)=r(f^{*})(x)=\delta_{x} \circ f^{*}=\delta_{f(x)}=f(x)
\] where \(x \in X\)
\(* \circ r = \operatorname{id}_{\operatorname{Mor}(A,\mathcal{O}(X))}\) as \[
((* \circ r)(\phi))(a)=(r(\phi)^{*})(a)=a \circ (r(\phi))=\delta_{r(\phi)(-)}(a)=\delta_{-} \circ \phi \circ a=\phi \circ a
\] where \(a \in A\).


We have now constructed all affine varieties up to isomorphism which allows us to establish the following categorical result.






ImportantClaim



Show that the category of affine varieties over an algebraically closed field \(k\) with morphisms is contravariantly equivalent to the category of finitely generated \(k\)-algebras with no nilpotents with \(k\)-algebra homomorphisms.


Recall the definition of equivalence of categories.
Given two categories \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{D}\), we say that they are equivalent if there exist funtors \(\mathcal{C}\xrightarrow{\mathcal{F}}\mathcal{D}\) and \(\mathcal{D}\xrightarrow{\mathcal{G}}\mathcal{C}\) such that \(\mathcal{F}\circ \mathcal{G} \simeq \operatorname{id}_{D}\) and \(\mathcal{G}\circ \mathcal{F} \simeq \operatorname{id}_{C}\). It is important to stress that equivalence is not equality; it allows objects to be isomorphic, not identical.
The following lemma is always useful to check that if two categories are equivalent:






NoteLemma



Given two categories \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{D}\) and a functor \(\mathcal{C} \xrightarrow{\mathcal{F}} \mathcal{D}\), \(\mathcal{C}\) is equivalent to \(\mathcal{D}\) if the functor satisfies the following two conditions:

Fully Faithful:
For any two objects \(A, B \in \mathcal{C}\), the map
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(A,B) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}(F(A),F(B))
\] is a bijection (a one-to-one correspondence). This guarantees that the structure of morphisms (arrows) is perfectly preserved.
Essentially Surjective:
For every object \(Y \in \mathcal{D}\), there exists an object \(X \in \mathcal{C}\) such that \(F(X)\) is isomorphic to \(Y\) in \(\mathcal{D}\), i.e.
\[
F(X) \cong Y.
\] This ensures that no structure is left out.









NoteProof of claim



Consider the functor \[
X \to \mathcal{O}(X),f \to f^{*}
\] Then we see these two categories are equivalent by the lemma.


In the first section we know that an open subset of a space with function is naturally a space with functions and the inclusion map is a morphism. In general let \(X\) be a subset of a space with functions \(Y\). Then \(X\) has an induced structure of a space with functions.






NoteDefintion



Explicitly give \(X\) the subspace topology. A regular function \(f\) on an open set \(U\) of \(X\) is a function of the following form:
There is an open cover \(U=\bigcup{X\cap V_{\alpha}}\) where the \(V_{\alpha}\) are open subsets of \(Y\) such that \(f(y)=g_{\alpha}(y)\) on \(X\cap V_{\alpha}\) where \(g_{\alpha}\) is regular on \(V_{\alpha}\).








NoteExercise



Check that \(X\) is a space with functions and the induction \(X\hookrightarrow Y\) is a morphism.








TipProof



Suppose that \(V \subseteq Y\) is open and \(g \in \mathcal{O}_{Y}(V)\). We expect that \(i^*(g)\equiv g \circ i\) is regualr on \(i^{-1}(V)=V \cap X\). Consider the values \(i^*(g)\) takes on this set:
for any \(x \in V \cap X\), we have : \[
(i^*(g))(x)=(g \circ i)(x)=g(x)
\]
thus \(i^*(g)\) is the restriction of \(g\) on the subset \(X \cap V\) i.e. \(f \restriction_{X \cap V}\).
Take the open cover \(U=X \cap V\) (where \(\alpha=1,V_{\alpha}=V\)) and \(i^*(g)\) coincides with a regualr function \(g\) on the intersection \(X\cap V\).


With this notation we have






Important 1: Theorem









TipDefinition of locally closed subsapce





A subset \(L\) of a topological space \(X\) is said to be locally closed at a point \(x\in L\) if there exists a neighborhood \(V\) of \(x\) in \(X\) such that \(L\cap V\) is a closed subset of the subspace \(V\). One says that \(L\) is locally closed in \(X\) if it is locally closed at each of its points.
Remark:
Let \(F\) be a closed subset of \(X\) such that for every point \(x\) of \(X\), there is a neighborhood \(V\) of \(x\) in \(X\) such that \(V\cap F\) is closed in the subspace \(V\); it then follows from Prop. 3 of I, p. 18 that \(F\) is closed in \(X\). On the other hand, it follows immediately that in general there exist locally closed sets that are not closed in \(X\).

Proposition 1 Let \(L\) be a subset of a topological space \(X\). The following conditions are equivalent:

\(L\) is locally closed;
\(L\) is an open subset of the subspace \(\overline{L}\), the closure of \(L\) in \(X\);
\(L\) is the intersection of an open set and a closed set of \(X\).





A locally closed subspace of a variety is a variety called a subvariety. A closed subspace of an affine variety is affine and in this case a regular function on the subspace lifts to a regular function on the ambient variety.








TipProof




A closed subspace of an affine variety is affine.

Let \(Y=\Spec A\) where \(A\) is a finitely generated \(k\)-algera with no nilpotents. A closed subset \(X\) of \(\Spec A\) is of the form \(\operatorname{zeroes}(P)=\operatorname{zeroes}(P\cdot A)=\operatorname{zeroes}(\sqrt{P \cdot A}), P \subseteq A\). Then clearly set-theoretically \(X=\Spec (A/\sqrt{P \cdot A})\). One simply checks directly from the definitions that:
\(\Spec (A/I)\) where \(I\) is a radical ideal of \(A\) has the induced structure as a space with functions.
Therefore \(X\) is affine if it is closed in an affine and clearly any regular functions on the closed subset is of the form \(f+I\) which lifts to a regular functon \(f\) (maybe not unique) on the ambient variety.

If \(X \subseteq Y\) is open and \(Y\) is an affine variety then \(X\) has a finite covering by open affines.

As \(X\) is open, \(X=\bigcup{D(a_{i})}\) where the \(a_i\) are in \(A\). Then the \(D(a_{i})\) are the affines \(\Spec (A_{(a_{i})})\). To see that there are only finitely many necessary \(D(a_{i})\) we use

Lemma 1
Any open subset of a variety is quasi-compact.










Note 1: Exercise



Let \(X\) be a subspace of a space with functions \(Y\). For any space with functions \(Z\) a mapping \(Z \to X\) is a morphism if the composition \(Z \to X \to Y\) is a morphism.








TipProof



Suppose that \(f : Z \rightarrow X\), \(i: X \hookrightarrow Y\) and the composition \(h=i \circ f:Z \rightarrow Y\). We expect to show that:
If \(h\) is a morphism, then \(f:Z \rightarrow X\) is a morphism.

\(f\) is continuous.

Let \(U \subseteq X\) be open. Then there exists an open subset of \(V\) such that \(U=X \cap V=i^{-1}(V)\). Then \[
f^{-1}(U)=f^{-1}(i^{-1}(V))=(i \circ f)^{-1}(V)=h^{-1}(V)
\] which is an open subset of \(Z\) as \(h\) is continuous.

\(f\) pulls-back regular functions to regular functions.

Let \(U \subseteq X\) be open and \(g \in \mathcal{O}_{X}(U)\). We want to show that \(f^{*}(g)=g \circ f\) is regualr on \(f^{-1}(U)\).
As \(g\) is regular on the open subset \(U\) of \(X\), by definition, there exists a family of open subsets \(V_{\alpha}\) of \(Y\) such that \(U= \bigcup_{\alpha}(X \cap V_{\alpha})\) and \(g=g_{\alpha}\) on each \(X \cap V_{\alpha}\) where \(g_{\alpha}\in \mathcal{O}_{Y}(V_{\alpha})\). Next we use \(f^{-1}\) to pull-back the open cover \(U\) to \(f^{-1}(U) \subseteq Z\), i.e. \(W_{\alpha}=f^{-1}(X \cap V_{\alpha})\) is an open cover of \(f^{-1}(U)\).
On each open set \(W_{\alpha}\) we consider \(g \circ f\):
When \(z \in W_{\alpha}\), we have \(f(z) \in X \cap V_{\alpha}\), thus: \[
(g \circ f)(z)=g(f(z))=g_{\alpha}(f(z))=g_{\alpha}(i(f(z)))=g_{\alpha}(h(z))
\]
then on each \(W_{\alpha}\) we have \[
(g \circ f)\restriction_{W_{\alpha}}=g_{\alpha} \circ h=h^{*}(g_{\alpha})
\]
As \(h\) is a morphism we have \(h^{*}(g)\) is regular on \(h^{-1}(V_{\alpha})=W_{\alpha}\). Gluing up all the local functions we know that \(h^{*}(g)=g \circ f\) is regular on \(f^{-1}(U)\).

title: The existence of affine varieties
text:
The main work of this section is to explicitly construct all affine varieties.






ImportantTheorem



If \(A\) is a finitely generated \(k\)-algebra with no nilpotents, then there is a canonically constructed affine variety \(\Spec A\) with a natural isomorphism \[
A \cong \mathcal{O}(\Spec A)
\]


Recall that \(A\) has no nilpotents(reduced) if \(a^{n}=0\) for some \(n > 0\) implies that \(a=0\) in \(A\). Since the \(k\)-algebra of \(k\)-valued functions is clearly reduced, the hypothesis of being reduced and finitely-generated is necessary for \(A\) to be an affine variety. Therefore this theorem constructs all affine varieties up to isomorphism. (for \(X \cong Y \quad \text{iff} \quad \mathcal{O}(X) \cong \mathcal{O}(Y)\))
As a set we define \[
\Spec A:=Hom_{k}(A,k)
\] Before giving strcuture on this set, we shall look at the \(k\)-valued functions on \(\Spec A\).
A \(k\)-valued function \(f\) which admits the following representation (which is straightforward to see that is well-defined) is clearlt a \(k\)-valued fucntion on \(\Spec A\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\Spec A & \xrightarrow{f} k \\
x & \mapsto x(a) \quad \text{for some} \quad a\in A
\end{aligned}
\]






TipLemma



There is a natural homomorphism \[
\begin{aligned}
\phi:A & \to \{k\text{-valued-functions on} \ \Spec A\}\\
a & \mapsto (x \mapsto x(a))
\end{aligned}
\]
By abuse of notation, we denote \(\phi(a)(x)=x(a)\) by \(a(x)\).


Let \(I \subseteq A\) be a subset of \(A\). Define \(\text{zeroes}(I):=\{x\in \Spec A : \phi(i)(x)=0 \quad \text{for all } i \in I\}\)






TipLemma



The subsets \(\{\text{zeroes}(I)\}_{I \subseteq A}\) form the closed subsets of a topology of \(\Spec A\).








TipProof




\(\Spec A=\text{zeroes}(\{0\})\) and \(\emptyset=\text{zeroes}(\{1\})\)
\(\text{zeroes}(I_{1}) \cup \text{zeroes}(I_{2})=\text{zeroes}(I_{1} \cdot I_{2})\)
\(\cap \text{zeroes}(I_{i})=\text{zeroes}(\cup I_{i})\)



So far we have defined \(\Spec A\) as a topological space (together with the homomorphism \(\phi :A \to \{f:\Spec A \to k\}\)) and we introduce the regular functions on each open set now.






ImportantDefinition



If \(U\) is an open subset of \(\Spec A\), a regular function on it is a \(k\)-valued function such that there is an open covering \(U=\cup U_{i}\) such that each \(f\restriction_{U_{i}}\) admits the form \(\frac{\phi(a_{i})(x)}{\phi(b_{i})(x)},a_{i},b_{i}\in A,x \in U_{i}\) where \(\phi(b_{i})\) never vanishes on \(U_{i}\).


Clearly \(\mathcal{O}(U)\) is a \(k\)-algebra and satisties the condition (a) of definition of spaces with functions. For condition (b) note that \(D(f)=\bigcup (U_{i}-\text{zeroes}(a_{i})\bigcap U_{i})\) is open and \(\tfrac{1}{f}=\tfrac{\phi(b_{i})}{\phi(a_{i})}\) is regular on \(D(f)\). Since \(\phi(a)=\tfrac{\phi(a)}{\phi(1)}\), the image of \(\phi\) is contained in \(\mathcal{O}(\Spec A)\), that is, \[
\phi: A \to \mathcal{O}(\Spec A) \subseteq \{f:\Spec A \to k\}
\]






NoteExercise



Show that, for any ring A, the set of nilpotent elements \(\sqrt{0}=\{a \in  A: a^{n}=0 \ \text{for some} \ n>0\}\) is an ideal. And check that \(A=\sqrt{0} \iff A=\{0\}\)








TipProof




Suppose that \(a,b \in \sqrt{0}\), we have \((a+b)^{m}=0\) for some \(m>0\) and \((ra)^{n}=0\) for any \(r\in A\). Hence \(\sqrt{0}\) is an ideal of \(A\).
If \(A=\sqrt{0}\) then \(1^{n}=0\) which implies that \(1=0\).Hence \(A=\{0\}\).









NoteExercise



Set-theoretically, what is \(\operatorname{Spec}A\) when \(A\) is the polynomial ring \(k[X_{1},\dots,X_{n}]\)? Same if \(A=\frac{k[X_{1},\dots,X_{n}]}{(f_{1},\dots,f_{n},\dots)}\) for some polynomials \(f_i \in k[X_{1},\dots,X_{n}]\).








TipProof




\(Hom_{k}(k[X_{1},\dots,X_{n}],k) \simeq k^{n}\)
\(Hom_{k}(\frac{k[X_{1},\dots,X_{n}]}{(f_{1},\dots,f_{n},\dots)},k) \simeq \{(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\in k^{n}: f_{i}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})=0 \ \text{for all} \ f_{i}\}\)









NoteExercise



If \(A\) is a finitely generated ring with no nilpotents, let a be an element of \(A\). Consider the homomorphism \(\phi: A \rightarrow A_{(a)}\), where \(A_{(a)}\) is a finitely generated \(k\)-algebra with no nilpotents (Why?). Show that \(\phi\) induces an isomorphism \(\operatorname{Spec}\left(A_{(a)}\right) \cong D(a) \subseteq \operatorname{Spec} A\) where \(D(a)\) is given the open subspace structure as a space with functions.








TipProof



\[
\begin{aligned}
\phi: A & \rightarrow A_{(a)} \\
      x & \rightarrow \frac{x}{1}
\end{aligned}
\] We have \(\frac{1}{a},\frac{g_{1}}{a},\dots,\frac{g_{n}}{a}\) generate \(A_{(a)}\) where \(g_1,\dots,g_n\) generate \(A\) since if \(x \in A_{(a)}\) then it admits the form \(\frac{r}{a^{k}}=(\frac{1}{a})^{k}(f(g_1,\dots,g_n))\) for some polynomial \(f \in k[X_1,\dots,X_n]\), i.e.  \[
\begin{aligned}
A_{(a)} & \cong \frac{k[X_{1},\dots,X_{n},t]}{(I,at-1)} \\
\text{If we say} \ A & =k[g_1,\dots,g_n] \cong \frac{k[X_{1},\dots,X_{n}]}{I}
\end{aligned}
\]
If \(A_{(a)}\) has a nilpotent \(\frac{x}{a^{k}}\), then \(x^{m} \cdot a^{N}=0\). Then \((x \cdot a^{N})^{m}=0\) which implies that \(x \cdot a^{N}=0\) and we have \(\frac{x}{a^{k}}=\frac{0}{1}\) by definition of \(A_{(a)}\).

As sets we have \(D(a)=\{x \in \Spec A:a(x)\neq0\}=\{f\in Hom_{k}(A,k):f(a) \neq 0 \in k^{\times}\}\) and \(\Spec A_{(a)}=Hom_{k}(A_{(a)} \rightarrow k)\). Consider the map \(F\): \[
\begin{aligned}
F: \operatorname{Spec} A_{(a)} &\rightarrow D(a) \\
y &\mapsto y \circ \phi
\end{aligned}
\]

\(F\) maps into \(D(a)\) since \(F(y) \in Hom_{k}(A，k)\) and \(F(y)(a)=y \circ \phi (a)=y({a}/{1}) \neq 0\). (\(y({a}/{1}) \neq 0\) for \(y(1/1)=y(a/1 \cdot 1/a)=y(a/1) \cdot y(1/a) =1\)). Define its inverse \(F^{-1}\): \[
\begin{aligned}
F^{-1}: D(a) &\rightarrow \Spec A_{(a)} \\
f &\mapsto (\tfrac{x}{a^{k}} \mapsto \tfrac{f(x)}{f(a^{k})})
\end{aligned}
\]
It’s straightforward to show that \(F^{-1}\) is well-defined and belongs to \(\Spec A_{(a)}\). Moreover we have \(F \circ F^{-1}=id_{D(a)},F^{-1} \circ F=id_{\Spec A_{(a)}}\) as maps between sets.

We have closed subsets of \(D(a)\) are of the form \[
\text{zeroes}(I) \cap D(a)=\{x \in \Spec A: i(x)=0 \ \text{for all} \ i \in I \subseteq A, a(x) \neq 0\}
\] which implies that \(I \cap (a)=\emptyset\). And closed subsets of \(\Spec A_{(a)}\) are like \[
\text{zeroes}(J)=\{x\in \Spec A_{(a)}:j(x)=0 \ \text{for all} \ j \in J \subseteq A_{(a)}\}
\]

Then do some calculus as follows: \[
\begin{aligned}
&F^{-1}(\{m:A \rightarrow k | a \notin \operatorname{ker}(m), \operatorname{ker}(m) \supseteq I\}) \\
&=\{h \in Hom_k(A_{(a)},k)|(h \circ \phi) (a) \neq 0 , \operatorname{ker}(h \circ \phi) \supseteq I \}\\
&=\{h \in Hom_k(A_{(a)},k)|h(\tfrac{a}{1})  \neq 0 , \operatorname{ker}(h \circ \phi) \supseteq I \} \\
&=\{h \in Hom_k(A_{(a)},k)| \operatorname{ker}(h) \supseteq \phi(I) \}
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore \(F,F^{-1}\) are continuous, thus homeomorphisms.

To show that \(h \circ F \in \mathcal{O}_{\Spec A_{(a)}}(F^{-1}(U))\) First notice that \(h \in \mathcal{O}_{D(a)}(U)\) has the form \(h(x)=\frac{a_i(x)}{b_i(x)},x \in U_i,a_i,b_i \in A\), where \(U=\bigcup U_{i}\) and the denominator \(b_i(x)\) vanishes nowhere on \(U_i\).

Take \(t \in F^{-1}(U_{i})\). Expect that: \[
(h \circ F)(t)=\frac{a_i^{\prime}(t)}{b_i^{\prime}(t)},a_i^{\prime},b_i^{\prime}\in A_{(a)} \ \text{where} \ b_i^{\prime} \ \text{vanishes nowhere on} \ F^{-1}(U_{i})
\] Indeed \[
\begin{aligned}
(h \circ F)(t)=h(F(t))=\frac{a_i(F(t))}{b_i(F(t))},F(t)\in U_i,a_i,b_i \in A \\
\frac{a_i(F(t))}{b_i(F(t))}=\frac{a_i(t \circ \phi)}{b_i (t \circ \phi)}=\frac{(t \circ \phi)(a_i)}{ (t \circ \phi)(b_i)}=\frac{t(\phi(a_i))}{t(\phi(b_i))}=\frac{a_i^{\prime}(t)}{b_i^{\prime}(t)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence \(F\) is morphism. Totally same for \(F^{-1}\).













NoteExercise



Show that the collection \(D(a)_{a \in A}\) is a basis of the topological space \(\Spec A\) and \[
D(a_1) \cap D(a_2)=D(a_1 \cdot a_2)
\]

U=\Spec A- \text{zeroes}(I)=\{x \in \Spec A: i(x) \neq 0 \ \text{for some} \ i \in I\}=\bigcup D(i)_{i \in I}
\]

title: Spaces with functions
text:
Reading Notes: Algebraic Varieties by G.Kempf






ImportantExample



Roughly speaking, different geometric objects (in our intuition) cannot be distinguished by their topological structures alone.
The complex plane \(\mathbb{C}\) is homeomorphic to the open unit disk \(\mathbb{D}:=\{z:|z| < 1\}\). But they are totally different if we care about holomorphic functions on them (by Liouville’s Theorem).


Thus, it is suggested that we should consider topological spaces together with specific functions on them. From my perspective,these functions can be seen as local coodinates of space which may take values in a field \(k\) and we expect that there are rules of calculus like classcial calculus in \(\mathbb{R}^{n}\). Precisely prescribling the behaviors of these functions to achieve this goal is difficult for me. I will, nevertheless, first introduce the definition given in the textbook.






ImportantDefinition



Let \(k\) be a fixed field, \(X\) be a topological space. The space \(X\) is called a space with functions if every open set \(U\) of \(X\) is equipped with a \(k\)-algebra, \(\mathcal{O}_X(U)\), of \(k\)-valued functions on \(U\), satisfying the following conditions:

Let \(U\) be the union of a family of open sets \(U_i\). Then a \(k\)-valued function \(f\) belongs to \(\mathcal{O}_X(U)\) if and only if every restriction \(f|_{U_{i}} \in \mathcal{O}_X(U_{i})\)
Let \(f \in \mathcal{O}_X(U)\) for some open set \(U\). Then \(D(f):=\{u \in U:f(u) \neq 0  \}\) is open and \(\frac{1}{f} \in \mathcal{O}_X(D(f))\).

We will call the functions in \(\mathcal{O}_X(U)\) regular function.


Condition (a) implies that a function is regular if and only if it is locally regular.1
1 We should state (a) in categorical language (gluing condition): TODO2 We should distinguish the characterization of open set \(D(f)\) with “bump function” on smooth manifold which also characterizes open set.So here can we use the pure algebraic structure \(k\)-algebra to recover a family of basic open sets of \(X\): TODOCondition (b) allows us to do division \(\frac{g}{f}\) of regular functions in the open set \(D(f)\) where the denominator \(f\) doesn’t take \(0\).This condition is equivalent to saying that stalk of every point of \(X\) is a local ring (\(R,\mathfrak{m},k\)).2






Warning



Consider \(X=\mathbb{R}\) with Euclidean topology and open set \(U \in \mathbb{R}\).Define that regular functions on \(U\) is the restrictions of polynomial functions on \(U\).This is not a space with functions! It doesn’t satisfy condition (b). Just take \(f(x)=x\) which is a regular function but \(\frac{1}{x}\) is not a local regular function on \(D(f)\)
Let \(Y\) be an open subset of \(X\). Suppose \(f\) is a local regular function on \(Y\), is there a global regular function defined on \(X\) such that its restriction on \(Y\) is \(f\)?
No! We have example.






NoteExample





Let \(k\) be an infinite field equipped with the co-finite topology(in fact, equal to Zariski Topology of affine line \(\mathbb{A}_k^{1}\)). \(\mathcal{O}_{k}(k)=p(t)\) where \(p(t)\) is a polynomial function.
Consider the open set \(k-\{{0}\}\) on which \(\frac{1}{t}\) is regular (condition b). Suppose that there existes a global regular function \(F\) such that the restriction of it is \(\frac{1}{t}\).Then \(F(t)t=1 \ \forall t \in k-\{{0}\}\) and this is impossible.



Therefore we should treat local and global functions carefully.








NoteExample



Consider the complex plane \(\mathbb{C}\) with Euclidean Topology and assign the ring of all holomorphic functions \(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{C}} (U)\) to every open set \(U\). This is a space with functions defined above since \(D(f) =\{u \in U:f(u) \neq 0\}\) is open and \((\frac{1}{f})^{\prime}=-\frac{f^{\prime}}{f^{2}}\) on \(D(f)\).
In the example above, we consider the zeroes of a holomorphic function \(f \not\equiv 0\) on a open set \(U\), denoted by \(\{z_{i}\}_{i \in I}\). Then \(\frac{1}{f}\) is holomorphic on \(U-\{z_{i}\}_{i \in I} = D(f)\). By definition condition (a), \(\forall f,g \in \mathcal{O}_{C}(U), \frac{f}{g} \in \mathcal{O}_{C}( D(g))\) which is a meromorphic function on \(U\) as we defined below:
Suppose that \(U \subseteq \mathbb{C}\) is open. A \(\mathbb{C}\)-valued function \(f\) is called meromorphic on \(u\) if \(\forall p \in U\), there exists an open nbhd \(V_{p} \subseteq U, g_p,h_p \in \mathcal{O}(V_{p})(h_p \not\equiv 0 \ \text{on} \ V_{p})\), such that:
\(f\restriction_{V_{p}}=\frac{g_{p}}{h_{p}}\)
We see that, in definition, the meromorphic function is always a quotient of two holomorphic functions locally and in the example \(\frac{f}{g}\) is meromorphic where we take \(f_{p}=f\) and \(g_{p}=g\) for every point \(p\) 3.
Conversely: Does every meromorphic function on \(U\) admit such a representation? i.e. suppose that \(\cup U_{\alpha}\) is an open cover of \(U\) and \(\frac{g_{\alpha}}{f_{\alpha}} \in \mathcal{O}_{U_{\alpha}}(D(f_{\alpha}) )\) where \(g_{\alpha},f_{\alpha} \in \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{C}}({U_{\alpha}})\), and further suppose that \(\textcolor{green}{\frac{g_{\alpha}}{f_{\alpha}}=\frac{g_{\alpha^{\prime}}}{f_{\alpha^{\prime}}} \ \text{on} \ U_{\alpha} \cap U_{\alpha^{\prime}}}\) (as functions) for all \(\alpha\), is there a quotient function \(\frac{g}{f} \in \mathcal{O}_{U}(D(f))\) where \(f,g \in \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{C}}(U)\) such that \(\frac{g}{f} \restriction_{U_{\alpha}}=\frac{g_{\alpha}}{f_{\alpha}}\) for every \(\alpha\)?
Yes! But it really depends on \(\mathbb{C}\) and it fails when the topological spaces are higher dimension complex manifords. Hence we omit the technical proof (depend on Werierstrass factoring theorem of Mittag-Laffer theorem).Therefore, we have:
\(\textcolor{blue}{\mathcal{M}(U)=\{\frac{f}{g}:f,g \in \mathcal{O}(U), g \not\equiv 0 \}}\)


3 Denote all the meromorphic functions on \(U\) by \(\mathcal{M}(U)\). This imlies that \(\{\frac{f}{g}:f,g \in \mathcal{O}(U), g \not\equiv 0 \} \subseteq \mathcal{M}(U)\).\(\mathcal{O}_{X}(U)\) is defined as a \(k\)-algebra consisting of \(k\)-valued functions above. This is kind of ac.hoc. Hence we may generalize this concept as follows, though it’s hard to pin down who invented it. It seems reasonable to the connection between the extension problems (such as analytic continuations).






TipDefinition



Let \(X\) be a topological space. A presheaf \(\mathcal{F}\) of sets on \(X\) is a contravariant functor from \(Top(X)\) to \(Set\).
\(Top(X)\): Obj:open subsets of \(X\) Morphism:inclusion map \(V \subseteq U\)
Recall that a contravariant functor satisfies the following conditions:

\(\mathcal{F}(\emptyset)=\{*\}\), where \(\{*\}\) is the terminal object in \(Set\).
\(\mathcal{F}(Id_{U})=Id_{\mathcal{F}(U)}\)
\(\mathcal{F}(i_{U \subseteq V}):=\mathcal{F}(V) \to \mathcal{F}(U)\)
\(\mathcal{F}(i_{V \subseteq W} \circ i_{U \subseteq V})=\mathcal{F}(i_{U \subseteq V}) \circ \mathcal{F}(i_{V \subseteq W})\)

Further suppose the following conditions hold, then \(\mathcal{F}\) is a sheaf:

local axiom: Suppose that \(U_{i}\) is an open cover of open set \(U\) in \(X\) and \(s,t \in \mathcal{F}(U)\). If \(s\restriction_{U_{i}}=t\restriction_{U_{i}}\) for every \(i\), then \(s=t\). (wlog. suppose that \(U_{i}\subseteq U\))
gluing axiom: Suppose that \(U_{i}\) is an open cover of open set \(U\) in \(X\), and if we have sections \(s_{i} \in \mathcal{F}(U_{i})\) such that \(s_{i}=s_{j}\) on \(U_{i} \cap U_{j}\) for evry pair \((i,j)\), i.e.\(s_{i} \restriction_{U_{i} \cap U_{j}}=s_{j} \restriction_{U_{i} \cap U_{j}}\), then there is a section \(s \in \mathcal{F}(U)\) such that \(s \restriction_{U_{i}}=s_{i}\) for each \(U_{i}\).



It’s straightforward to see that \(\mathcal{F}(U):=\{f:U \to \mathbb{C}: f \ \text{is holomorphic}\}\) and \(\mathcal{F}(U):=\{f:U \to \mathbb{C}: f \ \text{is meromorphic}\}\) are sheaves on \(C\) with Euclidean topology.






Importantspaces with functions VS sheaf



Condition (a) \(\Leftrightarrow\) local axiom and gluing axiom is straightforward.
As functions which are pointwisely defined, the local and gluing axioms are naturally satisfied (Just define the global function pointwisely). (But when the functions don’t agree on some intersection, like \(logz\) and \(\sqrt{z}\) on \(\mathbb{C}\), we cannot define a global function on the whole topological space. And maybe we should create a new and more natural underlying space to glue local functions)
In fact, the concept of Sheaf generalize local regular functions to local algebraic data 4. Provided the conditions (c) and (d), we can restrict data to smaller spaces. Provided axioms (e) and (f) we can obtain global data from local.
However, for general sheaves, \(\mathcal{F}(U)\) doesn’t carry any algebraic structures (\(k\)-algebra in spaces with functions).


4 “The concept of a sheaf provides a systematic way of keeping track of local algebraic data on a topological space.” — Hartshorne,Algebraic Geometry
Constant sheaf subsheaf skyscraper sheaf TODO







NoteExample



Let \(X\) be a space with functions \(\mathcal{O}_{X}(U)\). Suppose that \(Y \subseteq X\) and \(Y\) is an open set equipped with the subspace topology. Then \(Y\) is also a space with functions with the structure: \(\mathcal{O}_{Y}(U)=\mathcal{O}_{X}(U)\), where \(U\) is open set of \(Y\).








Important 1: Definition



5 A morphism \(f\) from \((X, \mathcal{O}_{X}(U))\) to \((Y, \mathcal{O}_Y(U))\) sends \(X\) to \(Y\) and pulls-back (\(f^{*}\)) \(\mathcal{O}_Y(U)\) into \(\mathcal{O}_{X}(f^{-1}(U))\) satisfying two conditions:

\(X \xrightarrow{f} Y\) is continuous.
if \(g(v) \in \mathcal{O}_Y(U)\) then \(f^{*}(g)(u)=g(f(u)) \in \mathcal{O}_{X}(f^{-1}(U))\).



5 We should consider all spaces with functions as a category (depends on \(k\) loose the condition that \(k\) is a field ?)Indeed, \(f^{*}\) is a \(k\)-algebra map from \(\mathcal{O}_{Y}(U)\) to \(\mathcal{O}_{X}(f^{-1}(U))\). Like above we should generalize it to morphisms between abstract sheaves:
\((X,\mathcal{F}) \xrightarrow{f} (Y,\mathcal{G})\) consists of the following data:

\(X \xrightarrow{f} Y\) is a continuous map between topological spaces \(X,Y\)
A natural transform from \(\mathcal{G}\) to \(\mathcal{F}\).

\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
f^{-1}(V) \subseteq f^{-1}(U) \subseteq X & \xrightarrow{\quad f \text{ is continuous} \quad} & Y \supseteq U \supseteq V \\[1.2em]
\mathcal{F}(f^{-1}(U)) & \xleftarrow{\hspace{4.5em}} & \mathcal{G}(U) \\
\Big\downarrow & & \Big\downarrow \\
\mathcal{F}(f^{-1}(V)) & \xleftarrow{\hspace{4.5em}} & \mathcal{G}(V)
\end{array}
\]


What are functions?
maps between sets + what structures

NoteEx 1.1.1



If \(k=\mathbb{R} \text{ or } \mathbb{C}\) and \(X\) is any topological space,then \(X\) has a natural structure of a space with functions. Just take \(\mathcal{O}_{X}(U)\) as the \(k\)-algebra of all continuous functions: \(U \to k\). Show that any continuous mapping \(X_1 \to X_2\) is a morphism.








NoteSol





Suppose that \(X_1 \xrightarrow{f} X_2\) is continuous and \(g:U \to \mathbb{R}(resp.\mathbb{C})\) is continuous. We want to show that \(f^{*}(g) \equiv g\circ f\) is continuous in \(f^{-1}(U)\). Let \(V \subseteq \mathbb{R}(resp.\mathbb{C})\) be an open set, then clearly \((g \circ f)^{-1}(V)=f^{-1} \circ g^{-1} (V) \subseteq f^{-1}(U)\) is an open set.









NoteEx 1.1.2



Prove that the identity of a space with functions is a morphism and the composition of morphisms is a morphism.








NoteSol





Suppose that \(X_1 \xrightarrow{f_1} X_2 \xrightarrow{f_2} X_3\) and \(g \in \mathcal{O}_{X_3}(U)\) \[
\begin{aligned}
g \circ f_2 \in \mathcal{O}_{X_1}(f_{2}^{-1}(U)) \\ g \circ f_2 \circ f_1 \in \mathcal{O}_{X_1}(f_{1}^{-1} \circ f_{2}^{-1}(U))
\end{aligned}
\]









NoteEx 1.1.3



Let \(U\) be an open space of a space with functions \(X\). Then show that the inclusion \(i:U \to X\) is a morphsim and if \(Y\) is another space with functions and \(g:Y \to U\) is a mapping, then \(g\) is a morphsim if and only if \(i \circ g:Y \to X\) is.








NoteSol





Suppose that \(i \circ g\) is a morphism and \(h(v) \in \mathcal{O}_{X}(V)\), then \((i \circ g)^{*} (h) \equiv h \circ i \circ g\) is a regular function on \(g^{-1}\circ i^{-1}(V) \equiv g^{-1}(V \cap U)\). We want to show that \(\forall f \in \mathcal{O}_U(V)=\mathcal{O}_X(V)\) (since \(U\) is open) \(f \circ g\) is regular. It’s clear since \(g^{*}(f) \equiv f \circ i \circ g\) is a regular function on \(g^{-1}(V)\).









NoteEx 1.1.4



Let \(f:X \to Y\) be a mapping between spaces with functions. Given open covers \(X=\cup U_{\alpha}\) and \(Y=\cup V_{\alpha}\) such that \(f(U_{\alpha}) \subseteq V_{\alpha}\). Show that \(f\) is a morphism if and only if each \(f_{\alpha}:U_{\alpha} \to V_{\alpha}\) is.








NoteSol





Suppose that \(f\) is a morphism. We have \(f^{*}(g),(g \in \mathcal{O}_{Y}(V_{\alpha}) )\equiv g \circ f\) is regular on \(f^{-1}(V_{\alpha}) \supseteq U_{\alpha}\). By defintion condition (a), \(f_{\alpha}\) is regular on \(U_{\alpha}\). Suppose that \(f_{\alpha}\) is regular and \(V \subseteq Y\) is an open set and \(v \in \mathcal{O}_{Y}(V)\).We have \(V=\bigcup{V\cap V_{\alpha}}\) and \(f^{-1}(V)=\bigcup{f^{-1}(V)\cap f^{-1}(V_{\alpha})}\supseteq \bigcup{f^{-1}(V)\cap U_{\alpha}}\) Then \(f \circ g\) is regular on \({f^{-1}(V)\cap U_{\alpha}}\)(since \(f_{\alpha}\) is morphism) and hence, by definition 1, \(f\) is regular on \(f^{-1}(V)\).
